speechtext: Read his speech.

I have read his speech very carefully, and if my hon. friend would read it, he would be obliged to admit that what I am saying is true ; and that shortly after the contract was forced through this parliament the men who forced it through were obliged to admit that practically everything that Air. Blake and his associates contended was true. I would ask my hon. friends opposite if they are not ready to admit that Mr. Blake was justi-

fled in condemning those features of the contract which were attached to the land grant ; and if the hon. leader of the opposition were here, I would ask him if he did not himself two years ago condemn the tax exemption feature of the land grant by proposing from his place in this House that that right of the company should be purchased-by proposing to give several more millions to the company to buy out another bad feature of. that contract, another right which should never have been given to the company ? And did he not, when in the North-west last fall, condemn the principle of land grants, when he declared that the future North-west province must be compensated for the lands alienated for federal purposes ?
I approve of the contract before the House because there is no land grant attached to it. The Liberals condemned the Canadian Pacific Railway contract because of the provision giving the company's property in the North-west exemption from taxation for ever. I challenge the hon. member for Botkwell, or any other member of the opposition, to stand up and declare whether the Liberals were right or wrong in their opposition to this perpetual tax exemption feature. My hon. friends are now dumb. Let me tell them that one of the ablest men in their party, Premier Haul tain, of Regina, condemned that exemption in the most effective fashion, by the Rill of Rights which he submitted to the government here less than two years ago. in which he demanded the abolition of the perpetual exemption upon the property of the Canadian Pacific Railway in the North-west; and if the Conservative party approve of that they condemn themselves. They condemn the provision which they put in the Canadian Pacific Railway contract in 1891, and which every day since they have been holding up as something that ought to be worshipped.
I approve of the present government's plan for a new transcontinental line because it embodies no tax exemption features, but will leave this great property which is to be created to bear its fair share of local taxation, together with all other institutions and properties in the country, towards maintaining progressive and modern government as regards education, public improvements, and so forth.
Blake and the Liberals condemned the Canadian Pacific Railway contract not because they opposed the building of the road. _ The Liberal government, from 1874 to 1878, had most irrevocably committed the whole Liberal party to the proposition of a transcontinental railway, and to the idea that the Pacific province must be connected witli the provinces in the east. The hon. member shakes his head ; but if he reads accurately the history of the last twenty-five years, he will know that I am speaking the truth when I say that the government of the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, from 3194
1874 to 1878, did commit the Liberals of Canada to the proposition that the Pacific province must.be connected by a railroad at the earliest possible date with the provinces to the east.

Is the hon. gentleman not aware that the Liberal party, as led by Mr. Blake and Mr. Mackenzie, refused to carry out the bargain with British Columbia, even to construct a transcontinental railway within ten years ?

It was, of course, a question of time. They may have taken the position that they would be able to do it only within a certain time. But what I say is absolutely correct, as the hon. gentleman well knows, that the Liberal party were committed to the idea that the road must be constructed. As an hon. friend reminds me, it was the Liberal party which entered on the work of making the surveys for the road. The route was practically all surveyed, and the line which the intelligent railway builders of the present day are following is the line which was surveyed by the surveyors of the Mackenzie government. Though I live on the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway, I am compelled to admit that it was located in the wrong place, and that it would have been very much better for the Dominion of .Cana da if it had been located in accordance with the surveys carried out by the Mackenzie government. The chances are that the success which we are having in the North-west to-day would have been achieved, to some extent at least, twelve or fifteen years ago if the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie had not been defeated in 1878 ; and the Canadian Pacific Railway would have been constructed and operated as a government undertaking. He already, when he went out of office, had important sections of the railway under construction. Why, Conservatives have gone up and down through the length and breadth of this country for years telling about the mistaken idea of Mr. Mackenzie. They did not take the position that he was not going to connect the Atlantic and the Pacific ; _ but what they said was that he had a mistaken idea about using the water-stretches. They talked about his senseless idea of water-stretches in combination with railways, but they are coming along very strongly towards that idea during this debate. Let me repeat that the contract of the Canadian Pacific Railway was not opposed by the Liberals on account of the original cost so much as on account of the monopoly and other bad features of the contract, which even the hon. member for Both-well (Mr. Clancy) dare not get up and commend. I again ask the question if Mr. Blake was wrong in his opposition to that contract ? The hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) read to this House amendments proposed by Mr. Blake and his associates in 1881, when the Canadian Pacific Railway

contract was being forced through this House. My hon. friend read resolution after resolution proposed in amendment to the contract. Will any lion, member opposite dare get up and say that, in a single particular, the Liberals were wrong l The Liberals in 1881 were twenty-three years in advance of the Conservatives of that day, just as they are to-day twenty-three years in advance of the opposition.

1 want to ask the hoi:, gentleman if it is not within his recollection that the Liberal leader denounced in the strongest terms the building of a railway to the Pacific coast ? Did not Mr. Blake declare, and in this he was cheered by every gentleman who supported him, that it would never pay for the axle grease V

It is perfectly true that Mr. Blake, in the heat of debate, in the heat of his opposition to the monopolistic and other obnoxious features of the Canadian Pacific Railway contract, did allow himself to go a little too far, and made the remark that the road would never pay for its axle grease, and the Liberals ever since have been sorry for it, and there are many Conservatives who for twenty-five years following this will be sorry for the disparaging remarks they have permitted themselves to make and for which they have not the justification or provocation which Mr. Blake-had.
The hon. gentleman cannot name one Conservative who made disparaging remarks concerning this country.
The bon. member for Hamilton himself told the House that there was a big section up there which did not have a tree as big as a man's thigh.
I never referred in that manner to the matter which Mr. Blake was discussing from first to last. I was discussing a different section altogether.

The hon. gentleman has entirely misapprehended what 1 said. 1 said that Mr. Blake did go too far in his disparaging remarks, and the Liberals have regretted it ever since; and I repeat that my hon. friends will be sorry, just as the Liberals have been, for the disparaging remarks they have made; and in that connection I point to my hon. friend's remark that there is a big section of country north of here, in New Ontario or in New Quebec, where you could not find a tree bigger than a man's thigh.

I said nothing of the kind. I said that the reports referred to by hon. gentlemen on the opposite side disclosed only the fact that there were certain timbers on the opposite side of the height of land; and they had no evidence to the contrary.
The hon. gentleman should thank me very sincerely for calling his atten-

tion to this remark and thus enabling him to make this explanation, because the impression has gone among the people that he said that the section of country through which it is proposed to run this road does not contain timber larger than a man's thigh. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) and many others made equally disparaging remarks regarding New Ontario and New Quebec; and I am perfectly satisfied that in the years to come they will regret the disparaging remarks which they made and for which they had not the justification that Mr. Blake had for making the statement which Liberals have since regretted. But respecting the position taken by the Liberal party, as shown by the amendments they offered to the Canadian Pacific Railway Bill, is there an hon. gentleman on the other side who dare get up and say that the Liberals were wrong in any particular V Am I not right therefore in declaring that the Conservative party themselves condemn the Canadian Pacific Railway contract ? There is not a man among them who would get up and argue that the ten per cent monopoly clause given the Canadian Pacific Railway was a wise and judicious provision. If he should attempt to argue anything of the kind, he would be looked upon as a violent lunatic. But I have here now the exact words which the hon. member for Hamilton did use regarding a section of the country through which this proposed line is to pass. But my hon. friend seems to have changed his mind considerably since last year. He asked in his speech on Friday night, why this hurry and anxiety ? After the government had been sitting here for seven years, he asked, what had occurred to make tills railway necessary ? He re-echoed liis leader by saying, why not deliberate ? Why this haste ? The hon. member for North Perth (Mr. MacLaren) last year said :
We have been for years talking, talking, talking. We have been doing nothing but talking, taking no action.
The hon. gentleman now asks, whence comes the call for action, for building this road ? I say it comes from the hon. gentlemen themselves, and from their leader- from scores of them who in this House last year and this year urged the necessity of immediate action, claiming that we were a year late already. So we are. But let me read what these hon. gentlemen said.
Did the hon. member for Perth refer to a transcontinental railway in that speech ?
I think not, but he was talking about the transportation question. He complained that we were doing nothing but talking ; and now my hon. friends want us to talk still further.
He referred to the canals.

The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) last year dealt with this matter a couple of times. As reported at page 4557 of ' Hansard,' he urged the government to prepare for the great emergency :
Prepare for the great emergency. Hon. members speak of the great crop of 1901, but I Have known three or four better crops in Manitoba. Last year's average was twenty-two bushels. I have myself grown twenty-eight bushels and we have had a better average in two or three previous years. Wo need not look to last year as anything exceptional. We are liable to have a greater crop at any time, and it behooves the government to prepare for a much larger export

On page 4392 my hon. friend is again reported as saying :
This is the burning question to-day. I said to Mr. Leonard : ' Provided there are no more railways opened up and we take merely the natural increase of the produce that will come from the people now in the country, to say nothing of the people now coming in, what are you going to do with the produce of that country six years from to-day '? His remark was ;
' Mr. Boyd, ten railroads will not take the produce of this country out in double the time you at present seem to think should he occupied.'
My hon. friend went on to say :
I say it will require four railroads between Fort William and Winnipeg, and two or possibly three more east of there to serve the trade that is looming up and is coming very soon in that country. What are you doing to meet the emergency ?
Tlie right hen. leader of the government lias brought down a measure to meet the emergency, and my hon. friend now turns round and takes the opposite position, and says we do not require any more lines to Fort William or east of Fort William. My hon. friend also said the other night that the congestion was now a thing of the past. Last year there was congestion, but now there is no serious congestion. Let me read a statement made by a coincidence, on the very day this debate commenced, the 10th of August,' by a gentleman whose authority my hon. friend will accept-Mr. J. T. Gordon, of the firm of Gordon and Ironsides, the well-known cattle exporters, and who is also a Conservative member of the Manitoba Legislature. Returning to Winnipeg from a western trip, he was interviewed by the newspapers there, and this is what he said :
We have shipped two trains so far this season. The first made a very satisfactory trip. I was present at Claresholme when the second train was loaded, and the run from that point to Moose Jaw occupied twenty-six hours. Owing to the cattle being so long on the road we were obliged to unload at Moose Jaw and the unloading and reloading occupied five hours. The accommodation at that point is very inadequate for the handling of range steers, as only two cars can be unloaded at a time. The cattle were reloaded at 23 o'clock Friday and at 20.30 o'clock Saturday had not reached the Winnipeg yards. If the Canadian Pacific Railway continues to handle western cattle in this manner we shall simply do as we did last year, drive the cattle south and ship over other roads. The Canadian Pacific Railway have appointed a live stock agent to look after these shipments and he is doing all in his power to give the cattle trains good transit, but he can only go so far. When despatchers and superintendents do not handle the stock in the manner suggested by the live stock agent and the shipper, then the shipper is surely justified in protecting his interest by going elsewhere. Our shipments over the Great Northern last year were very satisfactory. Instead of getting a 16 to 18 mile an hour run, as we are now getting from, the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Great Northern gave a run of 28 to 30 miles an hour.
'Does it cost any more to drive to the American roads ?'

'No. it will not cost any more, but instead will he a great saving ; _as it makes an enormous difference in the shrinkage when cattle are carried 28 to 30 miles an hour, instead of only 16 or IS. We can run the cattle across the line in bands of 1,500 or 2,000.'
I think the hon. gentleman will accept that as a satisfactory statement to the effect that the congestion is not entirely a thing of the past.	.
My hon. friend also said that if the government would only submit this matter to the people, and the people would endorse the government and the proposition, he and his friends would give it no further opposition. Except for the delay which has been too great already it might be worth while to take the hon. gentleman at his word. But when we look at the history of the past, I do not see why we should have any confidence in a statement of that kind. What occurred in the case of the Crow's Nest Pass Railway ? Every member of the opposition approved of the deal of the government with regard to that road, and the government went before the people, and the people endorsed it in the strongest fashion. But notwithstanding the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite supported it in this House, they still go through the country asserting that it was a bad deal.
With regard to the route proposed for the Grand Trunk Pacific, 1 have very little to say; I am willing to accept the evidence of Sir Sandford Fleming, the reports of the surveyors which have been quoted, and the evidence of such men as the hon. member for Renfrew (Mr. Mackie), who spoke from his personal knowledge after having travelled over hundreds of miles of that country. The evidence of these men satisfies me of the feasibility of the route. Mr. Speaker, the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway was found to be a more difficult thing than even was anticipated when the contract was put through ; but I will venture the statement that the building of this new road will be a very much less difficult thing than many hon. members on both sides of the House now think.
The north shore of Lake Superior for hundreds of miles is the most difficult country on the North American continent for railway building. The very worst possible route was chosen for the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I venture to say that that chosen for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will be found a much easier proposition. Here let me remark that the west is not the section of the country chiefly interested in this matter. The east is just as much interested. Nearly twenty years ago Sir John Macdonald remarked that you cannot check Manitoba, and that remark is just as applicable to-day to the whole of the country west of Lake Superior as it was to Manitoba then. Even if parliament should fail to build this road, hon. I gentlemen must not think that the traffic of

the country is going to be choked and that it will not find some other way out. Mr.* James Hill stands ready to-day to tap our western country with his Great Northern system at any point. This very session four charters have been granted from points in the territories running down to the boundary, and I am in a position to say to this House that Mr. Hill is ready to meet every one of these roads just as scon as it is built. !So that if this parliament should fail to do its duty towards the Northwest, in a very few years, possibly in a few months, the people of the North-west would get connection with the Great Northern Railway and the Northern Pacific.
As to the plan of construction, there were three alternatives before parliament and the people. First, to extend the government system ; second, to take no action and let private enterprise look after the matter ; and the third, to make a plan in conjunction with private enterprise and give the scheme a measure of public aid. The first plan, which involves tlie principle of government ownership and operation, *would have been the choice of the people of Manitoba and the territories. As to the second, it would have been in the last degree unfortunate for the west. Private enterprise could stand it, but the country could not. It would mean that the west would remain for ever in the grasp of the Canadian Pacific Railway, except for what relief it could obtain from American roads. As regards the third suggestion, as far as the people of the west are concerned, if they are not able to secure the adoption of the principle of government ownership and operation, the next best is a plan such as that proposed by the government. If we are not to have a government road, in my opinion, no sensible, patriotic Canadian can refuse to assent to a policy of public aid, because the alternatives are : On the one hand, continued progress and prosperity for every section of Canada anti every Canadian ; and on the other hand, an early check to the development now being witnessed, immigration discouraged and stopped, and some people now in and now going into the North-west Territories again on the road back to the States.
On the one hand, you will have continued development year by year of trade returns, exports and imports ; or, on the other hand, a return to the state of affairs of years gone by, when Canada's trade, foreign and domestic, was practically at a standstill. You will further have, on the one hand, a large annual increase of Canada's population, with the consequent annual reduction of the per capita amount of the national debt and lessening of the burden of taxation upon our present population; or, on the other hand, a return to a period when the number of our population was standing still year after year, with a national debt constantly increasing, and the burden of
debt constantly becoming heavier upon every taxpayer.
So that, while our western people would undoubtedly prefer government ownership and operation throughout, they are prepared to support enthusiastically the plan proposed.	.	. .
Let me quote on that point the opinion of a very warm advocate of government ownership, that of Mr. J. K. Mclnnis, the editor of an independent newspaper published in Regina, called the ' Standard.' Gradually public interest seemed to wane. The question of subsidies arose and the public began to stand back to see what would happen. To continue in that attitude' would be a mistake. Public opinion does not seem ripe for public ownership. The North-west cannot afford to await the maturity of slow and uncertain public opinion. We need a second line and we need it now. Railways are not built in a day. We are hard up against the realities of a continuous blockade and theories cannot relieve us. It seems, therefore, that it may he impolitic and altogether unwise to set ourselves entirely against the granting of some
public aid	
He concludes the article by saying :
It does not becpme Ontario and Quebec to object to western railway aid, so long as the North-west is the feeding ground of their manufacturers and they persist that our ocean bound traffic must pass their doors.
I wish to say just a few words on the question of wheat carriage. The hon. the Minister of the Interior made a speech on the subject before the House, which, I understood, occupied about four and a-half hours, and takes up about sixty columns of * Hansard,' and every page of the speech bristles with figures, facts and arguments in support of the government proposition. That these are unanswerable is proved by the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite have not attempted to refute them, except in two or three particulars. One of the arguments of the Minister of the Interior had reference to stocker cattle, in which he said the increase of railway facilities would promote the trade already existing between the eastern provinces and the North-west. On that argument some hon. gentlemen opposite have attempted to throw ridicule. But those who know anything about the

'vest and its possibilities will appreciate the minister's argument.
If the trade to-day were to be the measure of the trade two years hence, or ten years hence, I should join. hon. gentlemen opposite in characterizing the scheme as a mad scheme. But the importation last year of 50,000 stocker cattle-25,000 from Ontario, 25,000 from Texas-encourages me to think that in years to come, and to come very soon, that trade may multiply ten times over. It can never multiply without adequate railway facilities. The 50,000 head of fat cattle that we have annually exported for two or three years past, encourages me to hope that in years to come we will be exporting 300,000 head. If the Canadian Pacific Railway was unable to take out the 42,000 head that we sent last year, do we not need the ne# road to cope with the prospective traffic ? If to-day's traffic was not to increase, I should say, build no more roads, but compel the Canadian Pacific Railway, in return for Canada's enormous sacrifices in behalf of that system, to fulfil its obligations and handle the traffic efficiently.
The only statement made by the Minister of the Interior to controvert which any attempt has been made by hon. gentlemen opposite was his statement with regard to the wheat rate between Kansas and Chicago. The h'on. member for Peel (Mr. Plain) took exception to that statement, and said that the Minister of the Interior tried to delude the House with a bargain-day quotation. The minister quoted from the Inter-State Commerce report to the effect that wheat was carried from Kansas City to Chicago for 5 cents per bushel. I have here the report. In 1901, the commission reported :
Certain other conditions at Kansas city render it difficult to maintain the published rate upon grain, and the testimony clearly showed that these rates had not been observed. Dur ing the past summer the open traffic, Kansas city to Chicago, has been 12 cents per 100 pounds, but actual rale at which wheat has been moved has been as low as five cents.
The report of 1902 said :
The only published rate in effect January,
1901,	Kansas city to Chicago, was 19 cents on wheat and 16 cents on other varieties but grain, &e., habitually moved ostensibly upon the balance of the through-rate actually upon whatever rate the shipper could obtain by private contract with the carrier. The testimony before us showed that this rate varied greatly with the'stress of competition having been in 1901 as low as 5 cents per 100 pounds, the average being perhaps 7 cents or thereabouts. 1902.	this was reduced to 7 cents on wheat and flour, being retained at 12 cents on other kinds. August, 1902, 7 cents.
Tlie Minster of the Interior was showing *at what rate wheat could actually be carried under the stress of competition, and he in- '

stauced the rates that were actually Charged for moving vast quantities of wheat between Kansas city and Chicago. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) argued that the Grand Trunk Pacific could not carry grain to St. John from Winnipeg, all-rail, because the rate from Kansas city to Chicago was sometimes 14 cents. And I leave it to the House to say whether the argument of the member for Peel or the argument of the Minister of the Interior was the more intelligent one. I would support this scheme even if it could be absolutely shown that Wheat could never he carried over the the road. Until last year the Canadian Pacific Railway never carried a million bushels of grain all-rail to the sea-board. Last year was the first time they undertook the carriage or wheat all-rail in any considerable quantities. Yet, the Canadian Pacific Railway lias been a going concern, a very successful concern, and has been paying very handsome dividends upon a great deal of watered stock. If the west grows and sells its wheat, an enormous quantity of other business will have to be done. I venture to say we shall be producing as much as 400,000,000 bushels of wheat in the ordinary season before many years are over. Even if not abushel of that goes out all-rail, still, the Canadian Pacific Railway and t lie Grand Trunk Pacific and probably other roads as well, will have their hands full of traffic. But I am not by any means certain that such a road would not carry grain to St. John. The Canadian Pacific Railway carried last year about 2,500,000 bushels to St. John, and if they had had the facilities they could have carried 13,000,000 or 14,000,000 bushels.
Was that carried all-rail from Georgian Bay ports or all-rail from the head of the lakes.

The Canadian Pacific Railway carried about 2,500,000 bushels all-rail from Winnipeg to St. John last winter, and, as I say, they could have carried five times the quantity if they had had the facilities. We had the wheat to give them but they could not handle it.
Does the hon. gentleman know what price they charged ?

In the neighbourhood of 30 cents per hundred, I think. The Minister of the Interior showed, by quoting not merely the rates from Kansas city to Chicago, hut the rates from New York to Buffalo and the rates in force on the Canada Atlantic-actual rates, not bargain day rates, but the rates in force every day in the year-that with a road of equal stand-

ard it would probably be possible to carry .grain from Winnipeg to St. John all-rail for ten cents or eleven cents per bushel. Can the hon. gentleman give ns the rates to-day from Kansas city to 'Chicago ?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. ISlain) himself quoted the rate the other day and it was either 14 cents or 19 cents, I have forgotten which. But what does that prove? Did not the Minister of the Interior show that wheat was hauled from Kansas city to Chicago for five cents ? It does not matter whether that was a bargain-day rate *or not, millions of bushels were carried at that rate. On the Canada Atlantic, the maximum rate is 44 cents, while they have a minimum of 2| cents for a distance almost equal. The Buffalo and New York rate is even less than the Kansas city rate quoted by the minister. These are not estimates or calculations, they are facts showing what has actually been done under the stress of -competition. I think the Minister of tlie Interior said that the rate from Winnipeg to New York was about 164 cents per bushel at the present time, a Winnipeg grain *exchange man having so informed him.
That is the lake and rail rate.
If I remember well it was 71 cents from Winnipeg to the head of the lakes, two cents from the head of the lakes to Buffalo and seven cents from Buffalo to New York.

Yes, but I am dealing with the all-rail rate. The Minister of the Interior was showing what rate the grain could be hauled at all-rail from Winnipeg to St. John. He showed that, on a basis of the rates from Kansas city to Chicago, from New York to Buffalo and from Depot Harbour to Montreal, we might reasonably expect a rate of ten cents or eleven cents allrail from Winnipeg to St. John. As I said, if the Canadian Pacific Railway had had the facilities last year they might have hauled 12,000,000 or 14,000,000 bushels of wheat all-rail to St. John. And let me say to this House that it will never be possible for the whole crop of Manitoba and the North-west to be hauled out in the same season before the close of navigation. I see a statement in the paper to-night to the effect that Mr. Castle, the warehouse commissioner, stated in reply to questions that he did not anticipate any serious congestion
this year, and that about 65 per cent of the crop would be got out before the close of the navigation. The hou. gentleman at that time had no confidence in the government. Well, the position has changed at this moment. We were told by the hon. gentlemen opposite and by the ex-Minister of Railways that the Moncton end of the road was a piece of insanity. But the leader of the opposition is going to build it. I wait to bear tbe hon. member for East Grey say. When ? But he must have it under government control if he builds from Moncton to Quebec, and he says he will build it if a practical route can be found. Well, I am sorry that he is not so kind to the people of the west as he is to his constituents in the maritime provinces, for the people of Manitoba and the North-west are to be left at tbe mercy of the wolves of private corporations. er of the opposition is going to grant ruii-niiig powers to other companies. Yes.

I have occupied a great deal longer time than I had any idea of doing when 1 rc)se to speak, but I have done this, of cours'ev partly with the assistance of my hon. friends opposite, who have asked a number of questions. I would appeal to the opposition members of this House to rise above party-ism, to take a patriotic stand and to consider the whole interest of the people of Canada in respect to this project. I would appeal to them to assist the government in putting through this project that does afford some prospect of relief to the people of western Canada and does afford encouragement to the whole of Canada, to the eastern provinces as well as the North-west Territories and the western provinces. I would ask them to profit by history and not to let partyism influence their action-not to oppose this scheme simply because i|t has been introduced by the government, not to let partyism lead them into the mistake of Hon. Edward Blake of disparaging the country through which this proposed line will run. I believe they are satisfied that it will run through rich sections which offer encouragement for railway building. At all events, let them take into consideration the deplorable situation in which the settlers of Manitoba and the North-west Territories have been during the last two years

-conditions which have already been well described, and of which, I am sure, they are already aware. If there is nothing in the argument in the hon. leader of the government in regard to the bonding privilege, why are hon. gentlemen opposite so concerned about the allCanadian idea. Why did the lion. leader of the opposition, speaking at Toronto in March, lay such stress on the Canadian idea and on the idea of having a line that is an all-Canadian line, which will take the traffic in the winter to Canadian ocean ports. But now he comes down with a suggestion offering opposition to the plan proposed giving the shortest possible line between Winnipeg and the ocean ports. He comes down with an alternative proposition which will give a line 200 miles longer than that suggested by tbe leader of the government.
Fears have been expressed that the new project is going to injure the Intercolonial Railway. I do not to any extent share these fears. I am satisfied that the prairies alone, apart from the northern parts of Ontario and Quebec, will in a few years afford sufficient traffic to tax every possible transportation route that may be utilized, to tax the Canadian Pacific Railway, to tax the new Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, to tax a road to Hudson bay, to tax tlie road which will eventually be built through from the Peace river to the Pacific coast, and I venture to say that we will within a short time be doing a large business on roads extending from the territories and Manitoba into the country to the south of the 49th parallel, just as the people of the east are doing a large and profitable business with the people in the United States adjacent to their territory. I believe we are entering on a new era; we cannot judge the business of the future by that of the past or the present. Is there a man in this House who will not admit that if he had been told seven years ago that tbe development of the past seven years would be as great as It has been he would' have said that the prediction was simply a dream and a dream that could not be realized. I believe we are entering into a new era and that the business of Canada is going to grow from this day faster even than it has in the last seven years. We have in Manitoba and the west tbe greatest prospect of development that ever existed in any country, and I believe that the next 12 or 15 years will see in Manitoba and the Northwest Territories the most remarkable and

tlie greatest development that ever took place on this planet. I judge that from what has taken place in the United States. Thirty years ago the western states, that today have cities of 100,000, 200,000, 250,000 population, that to-day have industries representing millions of money, that have millions of population-thirty years ago these states were not as far advanced as Manitoba and the North-west Territories, as is western Canada at this moment. In thirty years they have built up these industries, these immense cities, these millions of population. I think that if we do in fifteen years what the western states have done in thirty years, we will be doing nothing more remarkable. Things move faster to-day than they did thirty years ago. Winnipeg today is less than one-half the distance from Liverpool that Kansas City was thirty years ago. Electricity as a force was scarcely known thirty years ago. At that time the western states had to draw immigration from the eastern states and Europe, and when the immigrants arrived they had to make their own experiments, they were not accustomed to the conditions. We to-day have these western states as a field for immigration. The people coming from these states are able to work from the first day they arrive in the country; they understand prairie conditions and can immediately go to work practically and successfully. As an illustration, I may state that the people in the weslei'n states spent years and years in experimenting to get a plough that would be successful on the prairies. Western Canada has the advantage of all the experimenting that has taken place in the last thirty years in the United States and it is not drawing too fine a picture at all to say that we will do in fifteen years what has been done in thirty years in the United States. If that is the case, it will be a very few years until the Canadian west will, as I said a moment ago, be supplying traffic sufficient to tax the capacity of every possible transportation route that can be provided.
I would say to this House, particularly to lion, gentlemen opposite, that this is a time to show courage, not a time to be discouraged; there is every reason for courage. Look back at the country west of Lake Superior as it was thirty years ago and we find not a single mile of railway. In these thirty years, even with the hampering effect of the policy of lion, gentlemen opposite, who were in power for such a long period, eighteen years, even with that we have made remarkable progress. Whereas thirty years ago there was not a mile of railway west of Lake Superior, to-day there are 5,000 miles of railway; in Manitoba there are 2.450 miles and in the territories 2,550 miles, over 5,000 miles of railway, and to-day there are being built westerly from Manitoba across into the North-west Territories no less than five distinct lines of railway. There

is the Areola branch of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which is an extension to Regina; then there is the ICirkella branch, which runs north of the main line; there is the Manitoba and North-western, which is being pushed forward at last, and then there is the Erwood branch of the Canadian Northern Railway to Prince Albert, and the Grand View extension of the Canadian Northern, which is being pushed on to Edmonton. Thus there are five distinct lines to-day being built into that country. But as I said if we simply build the lines on the prairie, feeders for the main roads, and take no thought for the spout, as Sir Wililam Van Horne has termed the section between Winnipeg and Port Wililam, and our own winter ports, then we will simply lead to further congestion. I support the proposition of the leader of the government because it enlarges the spout, a thing that has been talked about for years.
I would say in conclusion that this is a problem sufficiently large to engage the attention of all the people of Canada, a problem that is of interest to every section and every part of Athis Dominion, a problem which must be dealt with in a spirit of national enterprise, prudence and courage. It is so dealt with in the plan of the government, and I have no fear for the result. The plan is one that cannot fail, under the blessing of Providence, which, as hon. gentlemen opposite have been good enough to say, has been meted out to Canada in a generous measure during the regime of the present government, to promote national de-velofnnent, national enrichment, national expansion and national solidarity-.

Now, who is right, Mr. Speaker ? Surely the contention of this side of the House is reasonable, when we say we want a little more information on this subject. Why, Sir, it is ridiculous to think or to tell the people of this Dominion that 1,800 miles of railway can be constructed through the country through which this railway has to pass, or any other country, for any such sum as 513,000,000.
Then we have another in the person of the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir Wm. Mulock), who after a two hours' struggle to get the fly knocked off his back, he comes to the conclusion that the Premier's estimate is right, and that the road can he completed for $13,000,000.
Still we have another, this one is prepared by the Finance Minister. He seems to have gone into a calculation very minutely, as he gives the cost to a cent. What is his estimate? It is different from all the rest. He gives us $11,512,327.02. We would naturally think that the amount of the estimate given by the Finance Minister is correct. He is satisfied that it is, as he further adds, that this is the grand total, and that he has still a surplus of several million dollars left. By that expression, we would think, he was still on the lookout for larger and more extensive fields to spend the balance of his surplus.

mistaken once before. It will be observed that the Finance Minister is a very close tigurer. In referring to the cost, $13,000,000. or the lower estimates, $11,512,327.02, 1 am very much inclined to think that both the Finance and the First Minister are merely calculating interest on a suppositious amount. A settler who located not far from where I live in 1902 and who bought a section of land had in the first year 400 acres of land ready for crop. He is a prairie farmer from the south and lie will not be satisfied until he gets every acre under the plough. He represents the class of settlers who are moving from the United States to the North-west with all the plant necessary to put a large area under the plough ; and in a few years will have a greater development than those who went into the North-west in the seventies have achieved in twenty years. One American settler was asked by a customs officer at Winnipeg what induced him to settle on the Canadian side of the line. TIis answer was this :	I sold land for $40 an acre that
would raise ten bushels of wheat to the acre. I bought land in Manitoba for $10 an acre that would raise forty bushels to the acre. His reason was sixteen to one in favour of coming to this country. That man is not going to he satisfied with a few acres. He has come to raise wheat and he is not going to stop at thirty acres which the regulations require a homesteader to have under cultivation at the end of three years; hut will have every acre he possibly can under cultivation. I expect that the increase in the production of wheat for export during the next few years in the west will be something enormous.
Looking at the two schemes that are laid before us I think that I may say safely that the principle of affording relief to the west Is admitted. The government have brought down one proposition and the hon. leader of the apposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has proposed an alternative scheme. The scheme proposed by the hon. leader of the opposition involves a large outlay of money amounting to many millions of dollars and who will get the most of those millions ? Mr. J. R. Booth of the Canada Atlantic Railway will get a large slice of it and the rest will go to

the Canadian Pacific Railway, with no new country developed and no new land opened up. On the other hand the government's sciemo opens up an enormous new territory, it gives access to a new timber bolt, and it affords facilities to settlers on the prairies. It will give us a new line but I think that within a short time after we have that line built, the hopper of the west that we have been increasing from year to year will be so full and so large that we will be asking for another spout as the spout that we will have down the St. Lawrence to Montreal, Quebec and St. John will be handling all the business that it can handle. We will need another spout by way of Hudson bay and we will have to build another port at the magnificent harbour of Churchill.
